title: Groupoid completion preserves the nerve of an ordinary free category
statement:
Let $O$ be a small set and let $Q$ be a directed graph with vertices $O$, allowing loops, multiple edges and isolated vertices. Let $P(Q)$ be its free category: arrows are finite composable words of edges, identities are empty words, and composition is concatenation. Let $G(P(Q))$ be its ordinary groupoid completion, obtained by adjoining a formal inverse to every arrow and imposing inverse and composition relations. For an ordinary category $C$, write $NC$ for its nerve, whose $n$-simplices are strings of $n$ composable arrows. The canonical map
$$NP(Q)\longrightarrow NG(P(Q))$$
is a weak homotopy equivalence of simplicial sets [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper]. The assertion holds with no connectedness or nonemptiness assumption on $Q$.

source.place: Proposition 3.7, with D the identity-only category, and Sections 2.1,2.8-2.9 and 3.1-3.2, pp.269-272. This is an ordinary free-category theorem, not Proposition 9.2 about arbitrary cofibrant simplicial categories. No Stacks tag states it.

proof.text: Put $I=I_O$, the discrete category on $O$. For a subset $H$ of the edge set of $Q$, retain every vertex of $O$ and just the edges in $H$; denote its free category by $P_H$, its groupoid completion by $G_H$, and the canonical functor by $u_H:P_H\to G_H$. If $H$ is empty then $P_H=G_H=I$ and $Nu_H$ is the identity, hence induces the identity on every component and homotopy group. For an edge $e$ write $P_e,G_e,u_e$ for the singleton case. All these categories are small: finite words in a small set form a small set, and taking the stated relations is a set quotient.

source.place: Sections 1.4, 2.1, 2.3 and 3.1-3.2; the empty-generator case of Proposition 3.7.

proof.text: Suppose the unique edge $e:s\to t$ has $s\ne t$. Then $P_e$ has only $e$ and identities. In $G_e$ its component on $s,t$ has precisely one arrow between each ordered pair: any nonempty composable signed word alternates $e$ and $e^{-1}$, so cancellation reduces it to an identity, $e$ or $e^{-1}$, with the endpoints determining which. Every other object is isolated. Fix $b\in O$. In the comma category $(b\downarrow u_e)$ an object is $(a,\alpha:b\to a)$ and an arrow represented by $h:a\to a'$ satisfies $u_e(h)\alpha=\alpha'$. If $b$ is $s$ or $t$, there is exactly one such object over each of $s,t$, and exactly the arrow from the object over $s$ to the one over $t$, besides identities. If $b$ is any other vertex, the comma category has just $(b,1_b)$. Each of these categories is small and nonempty, any two objects have a common successor (the object over $t$ in the first case), and parallel arrows are equal and hence coequalized by an identity. By [lem-cbc-filtered-nerve-weak-contractibility] its nerve is weakly contractible. Thus $u_e$ is left aspherical in the precise sense of [lem-coef-grothendieck-aspherical-base-change]; that node's nerve implication proves that $Nu_e$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.

source.place: Proposition 3.7, one-generator case, expanded using the cited filtered-nerve theorem and ordinary Quillen Theorem A; Section 3.2 for signed words.

proof.text: Suppose instead that $e:s\to s$ is a loop. On $s$, the arrows of $P_e$ are $e^m$ for $m\in\mathbb N$, with addition as composition. In $G_e$ the exponent map to $\mathbb Z$ respects all relations; cancellation of neighboring opposite signs reduces every signed word to $e^n$ for a unique integer $n$ (uniqueness follows from the exponent map). Thus the arrows at $s$ form $(\mathbb Z,+)$, and all other vertices remain isolated. For $b=s$, the objects of $(b\downarrow u_e)$ are integers $n$, and an arrow $n\to n'$ is the unique natural number $m$ satisfying $n+m=n'$. Hence this is precisely the ordered-set category $(\mathbb Z,\leq)$. It is nonempty, has common successors $\max(n,n')$, and has no distinct parallel arrows. For $b\ne s$ the comma category is the singleton identity category. Apply [lem-cbc-filtered-nerve-weak-contractibility] to each comma category and then the left-aspherical nerve implication of [lem-coef-grothendieck-aspherical-base-change]. This proves the weak homotopy equivalence $Nu_e$ also for loops; no non-loop assumption is used later.

source.place: Proposition 3.7, one-generator case including the loop generator, with its comma calculation written out; Sections 2.1 and 3.2.

proof.text: For disjoint edge subsets $A,B$, assigning functors out of $P_{A\cup B}$ amounts to assigning images of the individual edges in $A$ and $B$, with the same specified images of their vertices. Extend to a word by composing its letters; concatenation makes this a functor, and uniqueness follows by evaluating every word. This identifies $P_{A\cup B}=P_A*_O P_B$, compatibly with all inclusions. Likewise $G_{A\cup B}=G_A*_O G_B$: every arrow in the latter free product is a finite word of invertible factor arrows, hence is invertible by reversing the word and inverting its letters. The functor from $P_{A\cup B}$ to this groupoid extends over its groupoid completion. Conversely the two inclusions into $G_{A\cup B}$ extend over $G_A,G_B$ and then over their free product. The two composites fix each edge and its formal inverse and hence every signed word, proving that these maps are inverse. Under these identifications $u_{A\cup B}=u_A*_O u_B$. This proves the particular free-product/localization identifications needed here directly from the presentations.

source.place: Propositions 2.2-2.3 and Example 3.2; elementary word/universal-property argument realizing the reduction in Proposition 3.7.

proof.text: We prove $Nu_H$ is a weak homotopy equivalence for every finite edge subset $H$, by induction on its cardinality. The empty case is step 1. For the induction step write $H=A\sqcup\{e\}$ with $|A|<|H|$. The induction hypothesis gives the result for $u_A$, and steps 2-3 give it for $u_e$. Compare the spans $NP_A\leftarrow NI\to NP_e$ and $NG_A\leftarrow NI\to NG_e$ by $(Nu_A,1_{NI},Nu_e)$. Their three comparison maps are weak homotopy equivalences. The maps $NI\to NP_A$ and $NI\to NG_A$ are monomorphisms: in degree $n$ the identity string at $o$ remembers $o$, so distinct vertices cannot be identified. The pushout clause of [lem-coef-sset-gluing-filtered-equivalences] therefore makes the induced map $w:NP_A\amalg_{NI}NP_e\to NG_A\amalg_{NI}NG_e$ a weak homotopy equivalence. Apply [lem-coef-free-product-nerve-gluing] to both pairs $(P_A,P_e)$ and $(G_A,G_e)$; its hypotheses require only small categories on $O$, so the second application is valid although these groupoids need not be free categories. It gives weak homotopy equivalences $j_P$ and $j_G$ from these pushouts to $NP_H$ and $NG_H$, using step 4. The canonical maps satisfy $(Nu_H)j_P=j_Gw$: both maps restrict to $Nu_A$ and $Nu_e$ on the two factors, so the pushout property gives the equality. Composition and two-out-of-three for [lem-coef-kan-quillen-right-proper] now prove that the actual map $Nu_H$ is a weak homotopy equivalence, completing the induction.

source.place: Proposition 3.7 and Lemma 3.8, printed p.272; finite-generator induction and its commuting pushout square expanded explicitly.

proof.text: Let $\mathcal F$ be the poset of finite subsets of the full edge set, ordered by inclusion. It is small and nonempty (it contains the empty subset); a finite family has its finite union as an upper bound. The two systems of nerve maps form a natural transformation $Nu_H:NP_H\to NG_H$, since inclusion of edge sets respects every defining relation and every canonical localization functor. Degreewise, $\operatorname{colim}_{H\in\mathcal F}NP_H=NP(Q)$: a finite string of finite positive words uses finitely many edges, and equality of positive words already holds in any subset containing their letters. Also $\operatorname{colim}_{H\in\mathcal F}NG_H=NG(P(Q))$: replace each arrow of a finite string by a finite signed edge word. This is possible because a formal inverse of a positive word is the reversed word of inverse letters. The union of the finitely many supports gives a finite stage representing the simplex. If two representatives become equal, their equality in the presented groupoid is witnessed by a finite chain of applications of the composition, identity and inverse relations in word contexts; all words in this chain involve finitely many edges. Enlarging to their union therefore witnesses equality at a finite stage. This proves both surjectivity and injectivity of the degreewise colimit comparison. Faces compose or delete words and degeneracies insert empty words, so the comparisons commute with every simplicial operator. They identify the colimit transformation with the canonical map $NP(Q)\to NG(P(Q))$.

source.place: Sections 2.1 and 3.1-3.2; finite-word and finite-relation expansion of the arbitrary-generator passage in Proposition 3.7.

proof.text: Every component of the natural transformation in step 6 is a weak homotopy equivalence by step 5, and $\mathcal F$ has exactly the small nonempty directed-poset hypotheses of the filtered-colimit clause of [lem-coef-sset-gluing-filtered-equivalences]. That clause and the explicit identifications of step 6 prove that $NP(Q)\to NG(P(Q))$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. This includes the empty edge set, when $\mathcal F$ has one element and the map is the identity of $NI_O$, and the empty vertex set, when both nerves are empty. No argument selected a connected component or a vertex of $Q$, and isolated vertices were retained at every finite stage.

source.place: Proposition 3.7, arbitrary small free category; filtered finite-generator passage, including empty and disconnected cases.
